title: Amazon — A configuration change in the Seoul region incorrectly removed the setting that specifies the minimum
summary: A configuration change in the Seoul region incorrectly removed the setting that specifies the minimum healthy hosts for the EC2 DNS resolver fleet, so the system fell back to a very low default. The fleet's healthy host count dropped and in-VPC DNS queries from EC2 instances failed for ~84 minutes until capacity was manually restored. AWS added semantic config validation and per-hour throttling on host removal as remediations.
fix: Restore DNS resolver capacity; add configuration validation and limits on host removal.

title: CircleCI — A deploy changed the type of a field in the PostgreSQL database used by the job-distribution service
summary: A deploy changed the type of a field in the PostgreSQL database used by the job-distribution service. Newly-written rows used the new type and old rows used the old type, so the distributor's strict schema validation failed on each scan and it stopped distributing work. Rolling back made the rows written between the two deploys unreadable, so distribution kept failing; recovery required hand-deploying a build that ignored the offending field, plus manual scaling.
fix: Deploy a compatible distributor build that ignores the changed field; manually scale the service.

title: CircleCI — An IAM-role gap permitted out-of-band changes to AWS WAF outside of CircleCI's Terraform pipeline; an
summary: An IAM-role gap permitted out-of-band changes to AWS WAF outside of CircleCI's Terraform pipeline; an operator performing what they believed were read-only investigation actions modified WAF in a way that began blocking legitimate traffic to the `api.circleci.com` and `circleci.com` CloudFront distributions. Because the change wasn't recorded in Terraform, responders deprioritized WAF as a suspect and chased CORS errors and recent deploys until automated drift detection surfaced the discrepancy.
fix: Reverted the problematic AWS WAF rule on both affected CloudFront distributions.

title: Cloudflare — A bad config (router rule) caused all of their edge routers to crash, taking down all of Cloudflare
summary: A bad config (router rule) caused all of their edge routers to crash, taking down all of Cloudflare.
fix: Removed the faulty router rule and had unresponsive routers physically hard-rebooted.

title: Cloudflare — During a maintenance of their private backbone network, an engineer made a typo in the Atlanta
summary: During a maintenance of their private backbone network, an engineer made a typo in the Atlanta datacenter network configuration, causing all traffic coming from America and Europe flowing to this only datacenter, crushing it.
fix: Disabled the misconfigured Atlanta backbone router so traffic could resume normal routing.

title: Cloudflare — A change to our Tiered Cache system caused some requests to fail for users with status code 530
summary: A change to our Tiered Cache system caused some requests to fail for users with status code 530. The impact lasted for almost six hours in total. We estimate that about 5% of all requests failed at peak. Because of the complexity of our system and a blind spot in our tests, we did not spot this when the change was released to our test environment.
fix: Rolled back the faulty Tiered Cache release across affected data centers.

title: Cloudflare — Several Cloudflare services became unavailable for 121 minutes on January 24, 2023 due to an error
summary: Several Cloudflare services became unavailable for 121 minutes on January 24, 2023 due to an error releasing code that manages service tokens. The incident degraded a wide range of Cloudflare products including aspects of our Workers platform, our Zero Trust solution, and control plane functions in our content delivery network (CDN).
fix: Rolled back the release and restored affected service tokens from a database backup.

title: Cloudflare — On October 4, 2023, a Cloudflare software error disrupted DNS resolution from 07:00 to 11:00 UTC
summary: On October 4, 2023, a Cloudflare software error disrupted DNS resolution from 07:00 to 11:00 UTC. Some valid queries to the 1.1.1.1 resolver returned SERVFAIL, affecting users of WARP, Zero Trust, and third-party resolvers that depend on 1.1.1.1. The incident was caused by an internal software problem rather than an external attack.
fix: Disabled the faulty static_zone application that was returning stale DNS information.

title: Cloudflare — On 18 Nov. 2025, a change in permissions in a database in Cloudflare's bot-detection systems caused a
summary: On 18 Nov. 2025, a change in permissions in a database in Cloudflare's bot-detection systems caused a file to be output that exceeded the limits of the software that runs that system. That file was propagated througout Cloudflare's network, causing a systemwide outage.
fix: Initiated a rollback of the change that disrupted Cloudflare services.

title: Cloudflare — A configuration change to disable an internal WAF testing tool propagated globally without a gradual
summary: A configuration change to disable an internal WAF testing tool propagated globally without a gradual rollout, triggering a Lua exception in the proxy's rulesets module that caused HTTP 500 errors for customers using the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset.
fix: Reverted the faulty WAF configuration change, restoring normal traffic.

title: Cloudflare — A bug in an automated cleanup task queried the Addressing API incorrectly, causing the system to
summary: A bug in an automated cleanup task queried the Addressing API incorrectly, causing the system to interpret all BYOIP prefixes as pending deletion and systematically remove them.
fix: Restored the deleted BYOIP prefix configurations to recover customer IP advertisements.

title: Cloudflare — Human error during abuse remediation inadvertently disabled the R2 Gateway service instead of a specific
summary: Human error during abuse remediation inadvertently disabled the R2 Gateway service instead of a specific endpoint, due to insufficient validation safeguards in admin tooling.
fix: Restored and redeployed the accidentally disabled R2 Gateway service.

title: Cloudflare — During credential rotation, the R2 engineering team accidentally deployed new storage credentials to the
summary: During credential rotation, the R2 engineering team accidentally deployed new storage credentials to the default environment instead of production by omitting the --env production flag, causing the R2 Gateway to fail authentication once old credentials were removed.
fix: Deployed the updated credentials to the production R2 Gateway Worker, restoring R2 availability.

title: Cloudflare — A newly deployed DDoS mitigation rule exposed a latent bug in the rate-limiting system where flawed
summary: A newly deployed DDoS mitigation rule exposed a latent bug in the rate-limiting system where flawed cookie validation logic caused HTTP request handler processes to enter infinite loops consuming 100% CPU, propagating across data centers.
fix: Performed rolling restarts of affected services and rolled back the newly activated DDoS mitigation rule.

title: Cloudflare — A deployment tool bug caused the production environment to reference a staging build version, routing
summary: A deployment tool bug caused the production environment to reference a staging build version, routing traffic to an unauthorized endpoint returning HTTP 401 errors, cascading failures across Workers KV, Pages, Access, and Turnstile.
fix: Manually changed deployment routes to return most traffic to the last known good build.

title: Cloudflare — A React component bug in the dashboard caused excessive API calls to the Tenant Service due to an
summary: A React component bug in the dashboard caused excessive API calls to the Tenant Service due to an improperly configured dependency array, overwhelming the system and cascading into broader API and dashboard failures.
fix: Reverted the problematic Tenant API Service changes to restore dashboard availability.

title: Cloudflare — An automated routing policy configuration error removed prefix list filters from BGP export policies in
summary: An automated routing policy configuration error removed prefix list filters from BGP export policies in Cloudflare's Miami router, causing it to advertise internal IPv6 prefixes to external peers and resulting in a route leak lasting 25 minutes.
fix: Manually reverted the faulty router configuration and paused the affected automation.

title: Datadog — A bad service discovery config in one of the clients brought down service discovery globally when a
summary: A bad service discovery config in one of the clients brought down service discovery globally when a dependent client went down.
fix: Datadog engineers corrected the faulty service-discovery dependency and restored the affected intake and web services.

title: Facebook — Configuration changes to Facebook's backbone routers caused a global outage of all Facebook properties
summary: Configuration changes to Facebook's backbone routers caused a global outage of all Facebook properties and internal tools.
fix: Restored backbone router connectivity across data center regions, then carefully brought services back online.

title: Firefox — On January 13th, 2022, a specific code path in Firefox's network stack triggered a problem in the HTTP/3
summary: On January 13th, 2022, a specific code path in Firefox's network stack triggered a problem in the HTTP/3 protocol implementation. This blocked network communication and made Firefox unresponsive, unable to load web content for nearly two hours.
fix: Disabled HTTP/3 on Google Cloud Platform to restore Firefox network connectivity.

title: GitHub — A Puppet manifest bug restarted only the authoritative nameserver (not the caching one) after an IP
summary: A Puppet manifest bug restarted only the authoritative nameserver (not the caching one) after an IP change, causing query timeouts. The deploy run during incident response then rebuilt the zone file from an internal provisioning API call that itself depended on DNS, producing a corrupt zone with `NXDOMAIN` for many records. Memory exhaustion from spawned processes on the fileservers extended impact to 1h35m of partial downtime.
fix: Restore the DNS zone records and recover the affected DNS servers.

title: GitHub — A configuration change rolled out to GitHub.com databases broke the way hosts answered routing-service
summary: A configuration change rolled out to GitHub.com databases broke the way hosts answered routing-service health-check pings, so the production read-only endpoint was marked unhealthy and inaccessible. With reads broken, the entire site was down for read operations for 36 minutes until the change was reverted.
fix: Revert the database configuration change.

title: GitHub — A telemetry gap caused security policies to be auto-applied to backend storage accounts in GitHub's
summary: A telemetry gap caused security policies to be auto-applied to backend storage accounts in GitHub's underlying compute provider, blocking access to critical VM metadata. All VM create/delete/reimage operations failed, taking out Actions hosted runners in every region, Codespaces, Copilot coding agent, CodeQL, Dependabot, GitHub Enterprise Importer, and Pages for ~5h53m.
fix: Rolled back the storage security-policy changes at the underlying compute provider to restore access to VM metadata and recover affected compute operations.

title: GoCardless — A bad config combined with an uncommon set of failures led to an outage of a database cluster, taking
summary: A bad config combined with an uncommon set of failures led to an outage of a database cluster, taking the API and Dashboard offline.
fix: Put the database cluster in maintenance mode, promoted the synchronous replica to primary, and directed applications to its IP address.

title: Google — Initial GCVE provisioning was performed with a legacy option, which lead to a 'fixed term' contract with
summary: Initial GCVE provisioning was performed with a legacy option, which lead to a 'fixed term' contract with automatic deletion at the end of that period.
fix: Corrected the system behavior that automatically scheduled affected GCVE private clouds for deletion.

title: Google — A configuration change intended to address an uptick in demand for metadata storage, which overloaded
summary: A configuration change intended to address an uptick in demand for metadata storage, which overloaded part of the blob lookup system, which caused a cascading failure with user-visible service impact to Gmail, Google Photos, Google Drive, and other GCP services dependent on blob storage.
fix: Stopped the configuration-change job and manually reduced blob-service traffic so crashed tasks could restart.

title: Google — Two misconfigurations, plus a software bug, caused a massive Google Cloud Network failure on the US East
summary: Two misconfigurations, plus a software bug, caused a massive Google Cloud Network failure on the US East Coast.
fix: Google redirected traffic away from affected regions, rescheduled the network control plane, and rebuilt and redistributed network configuration until capacity recovered.

title: Google — Google’s Front End load balancing service experienced failures resulting in impact to several downstream
summary: Google’s Front End load balancing service experienced failures resulting in impact to several downstream Google Cloud services in Europe. From preliminary analysis, the root cause of the issue was caused by a new infrastructure feature triggering a latent issue within internal network load balancer code.
fix: Google rolled out a change that disabled the vulnerable code path in its frontend infrastructure.

title: Google — Google Cloud Networking experienced issues with Google Cloud Load Balancing (GCLB) service resulting in
summary: Google Cloud Networking experienced issues with Google Cloud Load Balancing (GCLB) service resulting in impact to several downstream Google Cloud services. Impacted customers observed Google 404 errors on their websites. From preliminary analysis, the root cause of the issue was a latent bug in a network configuration service which was triggered during routine system operation.
fix: Fixed the underlying load-balancer configuration pipeline bug and restored customer configuration propagation.

title: Google — Google Cloud Networking experienced reduced capacity for lower priority traffic such as batch, streaming
summary: Google Cloud Networking experienced reduced capacity for lower priority traffic such as batch, streaming and transfer operations from 19:30 US/Pacific on Thursday, 14 July 2022, through 15:02 US/Pacific on Friday, 15 July 2022. High-priority user-facing traffic was not affected. This service disruption resulted from an issue encountered during a combination of repair work and a routine network software upgrade rollout. Due to the nature of the disruption and resilience capabilities of Google Cloud products, the impacted regions and individual impact windows varied substantially.
fix: Stopped the faulty network rollout and worked through a global rollback of the problematic configuration.

title: Heroku — An incorrect deployment process caused new config variables not to be used when the code required them
summary: An incorrect deployment process caused new config variables not to be used when the code required them.
fix: Sent the correct configuration variables to the instances and restarted affected processes.

title: Keepthescore — Engineers deleted the production database by accident.
summary: Engineers deleted the production database by accident. Database is a managed database from DigitalOcean with backups once a day. 30 minutes after the disaster, it went back online, however 7 hours of scoreboard data was gone forever.
fix: Put the site in maintenance mode and restored a DigitalOcean database backup, losing approximately seven hours of scoreboard updates.

title: NPM — Fastly configuration change caused backend routing issue.
summary: Fastly configuration change caused backend routing issue. To be exact, the issue is that we were setting the req.backend in a vcl_fetch function, and then calling restart to re-parse the rules. However, calling restart will reset the req.backend to the first backed in the list, which in this case happened to be Manta, rather than the load balanced CouchDB servers.
fix: The Fastly configuration was corrected to explicitly select the intended backend after a VCL restart instead of routing traffic to Manta.

title: Razorpay — A RDS hardware failure highlighted an incorrect MySQL configuration which resulted in major data loss in
summary: A RDS hardware failure highlighted an incorrect MySQL configuration which resulted in major data loss in a financial system.
fix: The RDS Multi-AZ failover automatically promoted the standby database; the application recovered after the failover completed.

title: rust-lang — On Wednesday, 2023-01-25 at 09:15 UTC, we deployed changes to the production infrastructure for
summary: On Wednesday, 2023-01-25 at 09:15 UTC, we deployed changes to the production infrastructure for crates.io. During the deployment, the DNS record for static.crates.io failed to resolve for an estimated time of 10-15 minutes. It was due to the fact that both certificates and DNS records were re-created during the downtime.
fix: Terraform completed the deployment and recreated the static.crates.io DNS record after the replacement TLS certificate was issued; DNS propagation then restored crate downloads.

title: rust-lang — On 2023-07-20 between 12:17 and 12:30 UTC all crate downloads from crates.io were broken due to a
summary: On 2023-07-20 between 12:17 and 12:30 UTC all crate downloads from crates.io were broken due to a deployment that contained a bug in the download URL generation. During this time we had an average of 4.71K requests per second to crates.io, resulting in about 3.7M failed requests, including the retry attempts from cargo.
fix: The team rolled back the faulty crates.io deployment, restoring correct crate-download redirect URLs, then fixed the missing URL separator and deployed the tested correction.

title: TravisCI — A configuration issue (incomplete password rotation) led to "leaking" VMs, leading to elevated build
summary: A configuration issue (incomplete password rotation) led to "leaking" VMs, leading to elevated build queue times.
fix: Corrected the configuration issue, restarted the service, and temporarily paused new builds while cleaning up queued VMs.

title: TravisCI — A configuration issue (automated age-based Google Compute Engine VM image cleanup job) caused stable
summary: A configuration issue (automated age-based Google Compute Engine VM image cleanup job) caused stable base VM images to be deleted.
fix: Travis CI engineers cleaned up unused images and restored capacity after the image-cleanup service had been disabled.

title: Turso — Incorrectly configured DB backup identifiers led to data leaks for free tier customers, and the
summary: Incorrectly configured DB backup identifiers led to data leaks for free tier customers, and the subsequent fix resulted in possible data loss.
fix: Reran the database migration with correct backup identifiers and recreated affected databases from their December 1 backups.

title: Amazon — An unknown event caused a transformer to fail.
summary: An unknown event caused a transformer to fail. One of the PLCs that checks that generator power is in phase failed for an unknown reason, which prevented a set of backup generators from coming online. This affected EC2, EBS, and RDS in EU West.
fix: Manually synchronized and brought backup generators online; removed failed management servers and paused EC2 launches in the affected zone.

title: Amazon — Bad weather caused power failures throughout AWS US East.
summary: Bad weather caused power failures throughout AWS US East. A single backup generator failed to deliver stable power when power switched over to backup and the generator was loaded. This is despite having passed a load tests two months earlier, and passing weekly power-on tests.
fix: Operators stabilized the backup generators, restarted the UPS units, and restored power to the facility before restarting affected systems.

title: Amazon — At 10:25pm PDT on June 4, loss of power at an AWS Sydney facility resulting from severe weather in that
summary: At 10:25pm PDT on June 4, loss of power at an AWS Sydney facility resulting from severe weather in that area lead to disruption to a significant number of instances in an Availability Zone. Due to the signature of the power loss, power  isolation breakers did not engage, resulting in backup energy reserves draining into the degraded power grid.
fix: Manually re-engaged power line-ups after safety checks, then used automated recovery to bring affected EC2 instances and EBS volumes online.

title: Amazon — Utility power was lost at a São Paulo AZ; during failover a breaker opened in front of one generator and
summary: Utility power was lost at a São Paulo AZ; during failover a breaker opened in front of one generator and a second generator independently failed mechanically, leaving the remaining healthy generators overloaded so they also shut down. The site's automated power-control system then malfunctioned, forcing operators to bring generators online manually. After power was restored, a network technician brought a device back up with a bad config that advertised an invalid route, degrading internet connectivity for both AZs in SA-EAST-1 for ~20 minutes.
fix: Operators manually brought generators online after the automated power-control system malfunctioned.

title: Amazon — A bug in third-party datacenter control system code caused excessive interactions during a control-host
summary: A bug in third-party datacenter control system code caused excessive interactions during a control-host failover, making the cooling control system unresponsive. Most of the datacenter correctly failed cooling into "max cooling" mode, but in a small portion the cooling units shut down instead, and the operator-initiated "purge" mode also failed because the PLCs controlling the air handlers had become unresponsive too. EC2 servers in one Tokyo AZ overheated and powered off; customers using ALB + AWS WAF or sticky sessions saw cross-AZ impact despite running multi-AZ.
fix: Operators reset the affected cooling controllers, restored cooling, and brought power back to the affected instances as temperatures fell.

title: ARPANET — A malfunctioning IMP ([Interface Message
summary: A malfunctioning IMP ([Interface Message Processor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interface_Message_Processor)) corrupted routing data, software recomputed checksums propagating bad data with good checksums, incorrect sequence numbers caused buffers to fill, full buffers caused loss of keepalive packets and nodes took themselves off the network. From 1980.
fix: Operators patched the IMP software to disregard routing updates from IMP 50, allowing the ARPANET to recover; they also planned a stricter routing comparison to prevent recurrence.

title: Cloudflare — A partial switch misbehavior caused a cascading Byzantine failure which impacted the availability of the
summary: A partial switch misbehavior caused a cascading Byzantine failure which impacted the availability of the API and dashboard for six hours and 33 minutes.
fix: Manually diverted eligible API read traffic to database replicas in a secondary data center to improve availability.

title: Cloudflare — Incorrectly set breaker coordination settings within the cascade safety breakers at Cloudflare's
summary: Incorrectly set breaker coordination settings within the cascade safety breakers at Cloudflare's Portland data center caused a complete power loss that bypassed all redundant power paths.
fix: Traffic and databases failed over to redundant infrastructure; over 100 databases across more than 20 clusters automatically restored service outside the affected facility.

title: Google — Successive lightning strikes on their European datacenter (europe-west1-b) caused loss of power to
summary: Successive lightning strikes on their European datacenter (europe-west1-b) caused loss of power to Google Compute Engine storage systems within that region. I/O errors were observed on a subset of Standard Persistent Disks (HDDs) and permanent data loss was observed on a small fraction of those.
fix: Automatic auxiliary systems restored power, and engineers manually returned storage systems to service and performed disk-data recovery; a small amount of recent data could not be recovered.

title: Google — On Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific, a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling
summary: On Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific, a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems in one of the data centers that hosts the zone europe-west2-a impacted multiple Google Cloud services. This resulted in some customers experiencing service unavailability for impacted products.
fix: Corrected the regional traffic-routing change that had inadvertently excluded all three europe-west2 zones.

title: PythonAnywhere — A storage volume failure on one of storage servers caused a number of outages, starting with
summary: A storage volume failure on one of storage servers caused a number of outages, starting with PythonAnywhere site and also with our users’ programs (including websites) that were dependent on that volume, and later spreading to other hosted sites.
fix: PythonAnywhere engineers recovered the failed file service using backup storage volumes while investigating the original volume failure.

title: Amazon — A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management left the regional endpoint
summary: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management left the regional endpoint `dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` with an empty record. Two redundant "DNS Enactor" processes raced when one was unusually delayed; a second Enactor applied a newer plan and ran cleanup while the first overwrote the regional endpoint with a stale older plan, which the cleanup process then deleted. The DynamoDB outage cascaded into EC2 (DWFM "congestive collapse"), Network Load Balancer health-check flapping, and Lambda for ~15 hours.
fix: Restored the DynamoDB DNS endpoint records; downstream services recovered as DNS caches expired and additional service-specific mitigations were applied.

title: GitHub — During an aggregation-switch ISSU upgrade, terminating an agent on one switch left the link up just long
summary: During an aggregation-switch ISSU upgrade, terminating an agent on one switch left the link up just long enough for the peer's MLAG failover to use the disruptive (rather than stateful) path, freezing the network for ~90 seconds. That spike caused fileserver Pacemaker/Heartbeat/DRBD pairs in different racks to exceed their heartbeats and STONITH each other, leaving many active/passive pairs with both nodes powered off; recovery required identifying the previously-active node from logs for each pair and took >5 hours.
fix: Identify the previously active fileserver nodes from logs and restore the affected pairs.

title: GitHub — A 43 second network partition during maintenance caused MySQL master failover, but the new master didn't
summary: A 43 second network partition during maintenance caused MySQL master failover, but the new master didn't have several seconds of writes propogated to it because of cross-continent latency.  24+ hours of restoration work to maintain data integrity.
fix: Restore database consistency following the network partition and MySQL failover.

title: GitHub — During routine ZooKeeper reprovisioning, replacement hosts were added too quickly and elected a second
summary: During routine ZooKeeper reprovisioning, replacement hosts were added too quickly and elected a second leader, creating two distinct ZooKeeper clusters. A Kafka broker for the background-job system connected to the new cluster and elected itself controller, so two Kafka clusters served conflicting state to clients; ~10% of background-job writes failed over 2h32m.
fix: Migrated background-job traffic and worker capacity to the secondary job-processing system; client retries and redundant queues helped absorb the backlog.

title: GoCardless — All queries on a critical PostgreSQL table were blocked by the combination of an extremely fast database
summary: All queries on a critical PostgreSQL table were blocked by the combination of an extremely fast database migration and a long-running read query, causing 15 seconds of downtime.
fix: The queued PostgreSQL migration completed after roughly 15 seconds, allowing blocked API queries to resume. The team subsequently recommended migration lock timeouts, shorter transactions, and splitting schema changes to prevent similar downtime.

title: Google — Many changes to a rarely modified load balancer were applied through a very slow code path
summary: Many changes to a rarely modified load balancer were applied through a very slow code path. This froze all public addressing changes for ~2 hours.
fix: Restarted load-balancer configuration jobs, allowing queued changes to process in batches and traffic to resume.

title: Google — A failure of a component on a fiber path from one of the central US gateway campuses in Google’s
summary: A failure of a component on a fiber path from one of the central US gateway campuses in Google’s production backbone led to a decrease in available network bandwidth between the gateway and multiple edge locations, causing packet loss while the backbone automatically moved traffic onto remaining paths.
fix: Google’s automated repair mechanism identified the failed network component and shifted traffic to restore service without manual intervention.

title: incident.io — Customers noticed their per-organization INC-N IDs jumping by exactly 32 (e.g.
summary: Customers noticed their per-organization `INC-N` IDs jumping by exactly 32 (e.g. `#INC-7` directly to `#INC-39`) after a Postgres HA upgrade that promoted a follower to primary. Postgres's `nextval` pre-allocates `SEQ_LOG_VALS = 32` sequence values on the WAL to avoid logging every `nextval`; a follower sees the post-crash state, so when promoted the sequence jumps forward by up to 32. Fix was to replace `nextval` with a `SELECT MAX(external_id)+1` trigger.
fix: Replace the sequence-based ID generation with a trigger using MAX(external_id) + 1.

title: WebKit code repository — The WebKit repository, a Subversion repository configured to use deduplication, became unavailable after
summary: The WebKit repository, a Subversion repository configured to use deduplication, became unavailable after two files with the same SHA-1 hash were checked in as test data, with the intention of implementing a safety check for collisions. The two files had different md5 sums and so a checkout would fail a consistency check. For context, the first public SHA-1 hash collision had very recently been announced, with an example of two colliding files.
fix: For affected Subversion repositories, deleting the problematic second file or adding an authorization rule to hide it provided relief; rebuilding a repository via svnsync was also described.

title: Azure — Certificates that were valid for one year were created.
summary: Certificates that were valid for one year were created. Instead of using an appropriate library, someone wrote code that computed one year to be the current date plus one year. On February 29th 2012, this resulted in the creation of certificates with an expiration date of February 29th 2013, which were rejected because of the invalid date. This caused an Azure global outage that lasted for most of a day.
fix: Microsoft corrected the leap-day certificate date bug in the Guest Agent, tested and rolled out the updated agent across production clusters, and deployed a corrected host-agent package to affected clusters.

title: Cloudflare — Backwards time flow from tracking [the 27th leap second on
summary: Backwards time flow from tracking [the 27th leap second on 2016-12-31T23:59:60Z](https://hpiers.obspm.fr/iers/bul/bulc/bulletinc.52) caused the weighted round-robin selection of DNS resolvers (RRDNS) to panic and fail on some CNAME lookups.  Go's `time.Now()` was incorrectly assumed to be monotonic; this injected negative values into calls to `rand.Int63n()`, which panics in that case.
fix: Deployed and progressively rolled out a mitigation for the leap-second-related DNS resolver crash, beginning with a canary node.

title: Mozilla — Most Firefox add-ons stopped working around May 4th 2019 when a certificate expired.
summary: Most Firefox add-ons stopped working around May 4th 2019 when a certificate expired. Firefox requires a valid certificate chain to prevent malware. About nine hours later, Mozilla pushed a privileged add-on that injected a valid certificate into Firefox's certificate store, creating a valid chain and unblocking add-ons. This disabled effectively all add-ons, about 15,000, and the resolution took approximately 15-21 hours for most users. Some user data was lost. Previously Mozilla [posted](https://web.archive.org/web/20250408175304/https://hacks.mozilla.org/2019/05/technical-details-on-the-recent-firefox-add-on-outage/) about the technical details.
fix: Deploy a valid certificate to restore Firefox add-on verification.

title: CircleCI — At peak Wednesday-afternoon load, the primary database backed up with queued operations to the point
summary: At peak Wednesday-afternoon load, the primary database backed up with queued operations to the point that it stopped catching up; rolling back recent changes had no isolated effect because the queue depth had already saturated the system, and a primary failover to kill queued ops only bought temporary headroom. After the runnable-queue was drained, builds were stuck in the prior queue stage; manually promoting them flooded the next queue, and the build-scheduler's failure-mode throttles fired on what were actually normal conditions and backed off precisely when more throughput was needed. CircleCI rebuilt tooling on the fly to clear a 17-hour backlog.
fix: Drain the overloaded database queue and restore stalled build scheduling.

title: CircleCI — A blue/green upgrade of the workflows database succeeded mechanically, but the post-cutover database was
summary: A blue/green upgrade of the workflows database succeeded mechanically, but the post-cutover database was running every query against disk because its statistics tables had not been updated. The team ran `ANALYZE` early in the upgrade procedure, but a second major-version upgrade in the same deployment then made those statistics stale, leaving the planner without usable indexes after the cutover. Workflows latency spiked, jobs were dropped after exhausting their 10-minute retry, and the team eventually re-promoted the old (blue) database to recover.
fix: Restore the previous database as primary.

title: GitHub — A schema migration produced enough load that Percona Replication Manager failed the MySQL master over to
summary: A schema migration produced enough load that Percona Replication Manager failed the MySQL master over to a node with a cold InnoDB buffer pool, which then failed back. Disabling Pacemaker `maintenance-mode` the next day triggered a Pacemaker segfault that produced a partition; two simultaneous master elections occurred and the elected primary was the stale node, allowing 7 minutes of data drift in which 16 private repositories were briefly routed to the wrong owners.
fix: Stopped Pacemaker and Heartbeat on both database nodes, restarted them on the primary node, and brought MySQL up as active; performance improved as its buffer pool warmed.

title: GitHub — The `mysql1` cluster experienced four ProxySQL meltdowns over nine days: an analytics query hitting the
summary: The `mysql1` cluster experienced four ProxySQL meltdowns over nine days: an analytics query hitting the master instead of replicas, a planned promotion that recreated the failure, and then two load-driven incidents revealing that systemd had silently capped `LimitNOFILE` from 1,073,741,824 to 65,536 because of a kernel-level limit of 1,048,576. Total impact was 8h14m across the four incidents.
fix: GitHub mitigated the overloaded mysql1 database and ProxySQL problems, adjusted ProxySQL file-descriptor limits, froze production deployments to stabilize the service, and partitioned data to reduce mysql1 load.

title: GitHub — A foreign key on the scoped-tokens table hit max INT32, causing high failure rates for Actions and Pages
summary: A foreign key on the scoped-tokens table hit max INT32, causing high failure rates for Actions and Pages and breaking scoped-token Git operations for 9h48m. Mitigation required a long-running schema migration to INT64. Linting that would have caught the column predated the column itself; one Action briefly received unauthorized access grants that were then revoked.
fix: Migrate the affected integer column to INT64.

title: GitHub — Peak-hour load on the shared `mysql1` cluster repeatedly exhausted ProxySQL connections over a week
summary: Peak-hour load on the shared `mysql1` cluster repeatedly exhausted ProxySQL connections over a week, requiring four primary failovers plus an emergency index and proactive throttling of webhooks and Actions. Memory profiling turned on to debug performance later triggered another connection failure, requiring yet another failover.
fix: GitHub restored database availability through primary failovers, implemented an index to address a high-load query pattern, and throttled webhook traffic to reduce peak database load.

title: GitHub — Two popular client apps had been quietly increasing read traffic 10×, then a Saturday change shortened a
summary: Two popular client apps had been quietly increasing read traffic 10×, then a Saturday change shortened a user-settings cache TTL from 12h to 2h. On Monday's peak, the combined write amplification from cache rewrites plus read load overwhelmed the core auth/user-management database cluster, cascading through every service that depends on it (github.com, API, Actions, Git over HTTPS, Copilot, etc.).
fix: Engineers manually corrected the database cluster state after failover left it without a writable primary; GitHub also prioritized load-shedding and architecture improvements to reduce future incidents.

title: GitHub — The GitHub platform encountered a novel failure mode when processing a schema migration on a large MySQL
summary: The GitHub platform encountered a novel failure mode when processing a schema migration on a large MySQL table. Schema migrations are a common task at GitHub and often take weeks to complete. The final step in a migration is to perform a rename to move the updated table into the correct place. During the final step of this migration a significant portion of our MySQL read replicas entered a semaphore deadlock. Our MySQL clusters consist of a primary node for write traffic, multiple read replicas for production traffic, and several replicas that serve internal read traffic for backup and analytics purposes. The read replicas that hit the deadlock entered a crash-recovery state causing an increased load on healthy read replicas. Due to the cascading nature of this scenario, there were not enough active read replicas to handle production requests which impacted the availability of core GitHub services.
fix: GitHub removed traffic from broken database replicas while they completed recovery, then returned recovered replicas to production.

title: incident.io — Two weeks of intermittent app timeouts, with traces showing requests waiting up to 20s for a connection
summary: Two weeks of intermittent app timeouts, with traces showing requests waiting up to 20s for a connection from Go's `database/sql` pool, but contention spread across many endpoints rather than a single slow query. After 24 deploys' worth of fixes (materialized views, indexes, lock timeouts, async Slack-webhook handling, and a custom `ngrok/sqlmw` middleware to attribute connection-pool hold time per operation), the root cause turned out to be an unnecessary transaction wrapping every Slack modal submission — many small fast transactions were in aggregate exhausting the pool.
fix: Remove the unnecessary database transaction around Slack modal submissions.

title: incident.io — After a Postgres 17 upgrade the weekend before, PGAudit was re-enabled based on staging testing
summary: After a Postgres 17 upgrade the weekend before, PGAudit was re-enabled based on staging testing. A routine migration to create an empty table and add an index triggered a pathological interaction with PGAudit: the extension hung while holding critical locks, ignored timeout signals, and blocked other DB operations across the dashboard, mobile app, Slack app, and API. The primary was restarted to break the deadlock (~2 minutes hard outage), then PGAudit was removed entirely.
fix: Restart the database primary and remove the PGAudit extension.

title: Amazon — Human error.
summary: Human error. On February 28th 2017 9:37AM PST, the Amazon S3 team was debugging a minor issue. Despite using an established playbook, one of the commands intending to remove a small number of servers was issued with a typo, inadvertently causing a larger set of servers to be removed. These servers supported critical S3 systems. As a result, dependent systems required a full restart to correctly operate, and the system underwent widespread outages for US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia) until final resolution at 1:54PM PST. Since Amazon's own services such as EC2 and EBS rely on S3 as well, it caused a vast cascading failure which affected hundreds of companies.
fix: Restarted the affected S3 index and placement subsystems to restore request processing.

title: Amazon — Message corruption caused the distributed server state function to overwhelm resources on the S3 request
summary: Message corruption caused the distributed server state function to overwhelm resources on the S3 request processing fleet.
fix: Amazon S3 engineers restored internal communication between storage servers and restarted request-processing components in the affected regions.

title: Amazon — Human error during a routine networking upgrade led to a resource crunch, exacerbated by software bugs
summary: Human error during a routine networking upgrade led to a resource crunch, exacerbated by software bugs, that ultimately resulted in an outage across all US East Availability Zones as well as a loss of 0.07% of volumes.
fix: Rolled back the incorrect network traffic shift, restored network connectivity, and temporarily disabled EBS control APIs in the affected Availability Zone while stabilizing and recovering volumes.

title: Amazon — Inability to contact a data collection server triggered a latent memory leak bug in the reporting agent
summary: Inability to contact a data collection server triggered a latent memory leak bug in the reporting agent on the storage servers. And there is no graceful degradation handling, thus the reporting agent continuously contacted the collection server in a way that slowly consumed system memory. Also the monitoring system failed to alarm this EBS server's memory leak, also EBS servers generally make very dynamic use of all memory. By Monday morning, the rate of memory loss became quite high and confused enough memory on the affected storage servers which cannot keep with the request handling process. This error got further severed by the inability to do the failover, which resulted in the outage.
fix: AWS engineers freed excess memory on affected EBS servers, allowing stuck volumes to recover and resume normal performance.

title: Amazon — Elastic Load Balancer ran into problems when "a maintenance process that was inadvertently run against
summary: Elastic Load Balancer ran into problems when "a maintenance process that was inadvertently run against the production ELB state data".
fix: Restored a snapshot of the ELB state data from before the accidental deletion and merged subsequent state changes.

title: Amazon — A "network disruption" caused metadata services to experience load that caused response times to exceed
summary: A "network disruption" caused metadata services to experience load that caused response times to exceed timeout values, causing storage nodes to take themselves down. Nodes that took themselves down continued to retry, ensuring that load on metadata services couldn't decrease.
fix: Reduced load on DynamoDB metadata services and gradually restored metadata partitions and normal customer request traffic; dependent AWS services recovered as DynamoDB error rates fell.

title: Amazon — Scaling the front-end cache fleet for Kinesis caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the
summary: Scaling the front-end cache fleet for Kinesis caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an operating system configuration. Multiple critical downstream services affected, from Cognito to Lambda to CloudWatch.
fix: Adjusted the Kinesis front-end fleet configuration and restarted front-end servers in groups to restore request processing.

title: Amazon — At 7:30 AM PST, an automated activity to scale capacity of one of the AWS services hosted in the main
summary: At 7:30 AM PST, an automated activity to scale capacity of one of the AWS services hosted in the main AWS network triggered an unexpected behavior from a large number of clients inside the internal network. This resulted in a large surge of connection activity that overwhelmed the networking devices between the internal network and the main AWS network, resulting in delays for communication between these networks. These delays increased latency and errors for services communicating between these networks, resulting in even more connection attempts and retries. This led to persistent congestion and performance issues on the devices connecting the two networks.
fix: AWS rerouted traffic away from congested paths, isolated heavy traffic sources, disabled high-volume services, and added network capacity until devices recovered.

title: Amazon — Multiple SimpleDB storage nodes lost power simultaneously in one US-East data center.
summary: Multiple SimpleDB storage nodes lost power simultaneously in one US-East data center. The lock service de-registered them rapidly, which spiked load and pushed handshake latencies above SimpleDB's too-aggressive handshake timeout. Healthy storage and metadata nodes failed their handshakes, removed themselves from the cluster, and couldn't rejoin because the metadata nodes that would authorize them had also taken themselves out. Recovery required manually raising the handshake timeout and restarting metadata nodes.
fix: Increase the handshake timeout and restart the metadata nodes.

title: Amazon — A new failover-optimization protocol had been enabled in network device OS for 8 months without issue
summary: A new failover-optimization protocol had been enabled in network device OS for 8 months without issue. A customer traffic pattern produced packets matching a very specific signature that triggered a latent defect in the OS, causing devices in one Direct Connect network layer to fail. Failed devices weren't automatically removed from service, so engineers manually drained them, only for additional devices to fail with the same bug. Disabling the new protocol restored Direct Connect to Tokyo after ~6 hours.
fix: Disable the failover-optimization protocol on affected network devices.

title: Amazon — As the Lambda Frontend fleet scaled in response to normal daily traffic growth, it crossed a capacity
summary: As the Lambda Frontend fleet scaled in response to normal daily traffic growth, it crossed a capacity threshold within a single cell that had never been reached before, triggering a latent software defect that caused Execution Environments to be successfully allocated but never fully utilized. Lambda invocations failed in the affected cell, cascading into STS, EKS, EventBridge, Connect, and the AWS Management Console for several hours.
fix: Disabled the triggering Lambda frontend scaling activities and deployed a fix for the latent bug.

title: Amazon — A Kinesis cell newly migrated to a new architecture had an unusually high number of very low-throughput
summary: A Kinesis cell newly migrated to a new architecture had an unusually high number of very low-throughput shards. The cell management system distributed the shards unevenly, so a few hosts ended up handling huge numbers of shards and produced abnormally large status messages. The system misinterpreted slow status messages as host failures, kicked off a redistribution storm, and overloaded the secure-connection provisioning subsystem. CloudWatch Logs, S3 event notifications, Firehose, ECS, Lambda, Redshift, MWAA, and Glue all degraded for ~7 hours.
fix: Added capacity to the secure-connection provisioning subsystem until the affected Kinesis cell could process requests normally.

title: AppNexus — A double free revealed by a database update caused all "impression bus" servers to crash simultaneously
summary: A double free revealed by a database update caused all "impression bus" servers to crash simultaneously. This wasn't caught in staging and made it into production because a time delay is required to trigger the bug, and the staging period didn't have a built-in delay.
fix: AppNexus restored capacity in its Amsterdam data center from a fresh internal database snapshot and deployed a tested fix for the crashing component.

title: Atlassian — On Tuesday, April 5th, 2022, starting at 7:38 UTC, 775 Atlassian customers lost access to their
summary: On Tuesday, April 5th, 2022, starting at 7:38 UTC, 775 Atlassian customers lost access to their Atlassian products. The outage spanned up to 14 days for a subset of these customers, with the first set of customers being restored on April 8th and all customer sites progressively restored by April 18th.
fix: Atlassian teams restored deleted customer sites through coordinated recovery workstreams, validated the restored sites, and returned them to customers.

title: Basecamp — Basecamp's network was under a DDoS attack during a 100-minute window on March 24, 2014
summary: Basecamp's network was under a DDoS attack during a 100-minute window on March 24, 2014. Same-day announcement that the attack was in progress: [signalvnoise.com](https://signalvnoise.com/posts/3728-basecamp-was-under-network-attack-this-morning).
fix: Filtered attack traffic through a single provider and coordinated removal of bogus DDoS traffic.

title: Basecamp — In November 2018 a database hit the integer limit, leaving the service in read-only mode
summary: In November 2018 a database hit the integer limit, leaving the service in read-only mode. Same-day status update during the incident: [signalvnoise.com](https://web.archive.org/web/20220530044506/https://m.signalvnoise.com/update-on-basecamp-3-being-stuck-in-read-only-as-of-nov-8-922am-cst/).
fix: Expanded the database event-table identifier capacity from a 32-bit integer limit to a 64-bit integer range, allowing Basecamp to resume writes.

title: BBC Online — In July 2014, BBC Online experienced a very long outage of several of its popular online services
summary: In July 2014, BBC Online experienced a very long outage of several of its popular online services including the BBC iPlayer. When the database backend was overloaded, it had started to throttle requests from various services. Services that hadn't cached the database responses locally began timing out and eventually failed completely.
fix: Restored the caching layer and used an emergency simplified homepage while stabilizing the affected backend services.

title: Bintray — In July 2017 several malicious Maven packages were included in JCenter with an impersonation attack
summary: In July 2017 several malicious Maven packages were included in JCenter with an impersonation attack. Those packages lived in JCenter for over a year and supposedly affected several Android apps that resulted in having malware code injected by those dependencies from JCenter.
fix: Banned the impersonating Bintray user and removed their malicious packages and JCenter links.

title: Buildkite — Database capacity downgrade in an attempt to minimise AWS spend resulted in lack of capacity to support
summary: Database capacity downgrade in an attempt to minimise AWS spend resulted in lack of capacity to support Buildkite customers at peak, leading to cascading collapse of dependent servers.
fix: Reverted to the previously working per-host PgBouncer connection-pooling setup.

title: Bungie — Side effects of a bug fix for wrong timestamps causes data loss; server misconfiguration for the hotfix
summary: Side effects of a bug fix for wrong timestamps causes data loss; server misconfiguration for the hotfix causes the data loss to reappear in several servers in a following update.
fix: Restored all affected character data from a backup taken before the faulty patch was deployed.

title: Chef.io — The recipe community site Supermarket crashed two hours after launch due to intermittent
summary: The recipe community site Supermarket crashed two hours after launch due to intermittent unresponsiveness and increased latency. One of the main reasons for failure identified in the post mortem was very low health check timeouts.
fix: The team stabilized Supermarket by adding application servers and upgrading their instance size, moving to five m3.xlarge instances. They also planned improved load handling, health checks, and alerting.

title: CircleCI — A GitHub outage and recovery caused an unexpectedly large incoming load.
summary: A GitHub outage and recovery caused an unexpectedly large incoming load. For reasons that aren't specified, a large load causes CircleCI's queue system to slow down, in this case to handling one transaction per minute.
fix: Disabled automatic build requeueing, drained database-backed queues, and then resumed builds.

title: CircleCI — By January 4, 2023, our internal investigation had determined the scope of the intrusion by the
summary: By January 4, 2023, our internal investigation had determined the scope of the intrusion by the unauthorized third party and the entry path of the attack. To date, we have learned that an unauthorized third party leveraged malware deployed to a CircleCI engineer’s laptop in order to steal a valid, 2FA-backed SSO session. This machine was compromised on December 16, 2022. The malware was not detected by our antivirus software. Our investigation indicates that the malware was able to execute session cookie theft, enabling them to impersonate the targeted employee in a remote location and then escalate access to a subset of our production systems.
fix: CircleCI rotated potentially exposed production hosts and GitHub OAuth tokens, revoked project and personal API tokens, and coordinated Bitbucket token rotation to contain the security incident.

title: CircleCI — CircleCI's database provider, MongoHQ, was breached on October 27, 2013, and CircleCI's MongoDB was
summary: CircleCI's database provider, MongoHQ, was breached on October 27, 2013, and CircleCI's MongoDB was among the databases accessed; CircleCI was holding GitHub OAuth tokens, Heroku API tokens, AWS IAM keys, and SSH deploy/user keys for customers in that database. On notification, CircleCI shut down the site and all builds, then worked with GitHub, Heroku, and AWS to revoke every OAuth token, API token, IAM key, and SSH key it had handed out, and cycled all of its own keys and caches.
fix: Shut down builds and the site as a precaution after the MongoHQ breach, revoked accessible SSH keys and API tokens, and coordinated revocation of compromised credentials with upstream providers.

title: CircleCI — Slow queries on the MongoDB replica sets backing the build queue caused workflows to back up over a
summary: Slow queries on the MongoDB replica sets backing the build queue caused workflows to back up over a two-week run of incidents. A roughly concurrent minor-version JVM upgrade enabled Docker-awareness by default, which silently shrank thread and connection pools across most JVM services and constrained throughput, masking the underlying MongoDB capacity problem. Tuning thread/connection pools and upsizing MongoDB stabilized the platform after multiple cascading outages on March 26, April 2, April 3, and April 10.
fix: Tune thread and connection pools and increase MongoDB capacity.

title: CircleCI — A routine RabbitMQ upgrade from 3.8.9 to 3.8.16 introduced a 15-minute consumer ack timeout that the
summary: A routine RabbitMQ upgrade from 3.8.9 to 3.8.16 introduced a 15-minute consumer ack timeout that the changelog described as scoped to quorum queues but actually applied to all queue types. Consumers on the VM-destroyer queue gradually got their channels closed until the queue had zero consumers, so VMs in one region stopped being deleted; this eventually backed up VM creation and blocked Docker, machine, Windows, Mac, Arm, GPU, and remote-Docker jobs for ~12 hours.
fix: CircleCI restarted VM service deployments to restore RabbitMQ queue consumers, increased GCP quotas and database capacity, shed job load, and gradually restarted provisioning and distribution components after queues drained.

title: CircleCI — A staged Kubernetes upgrade of CircleCI's main production cluster left `kube-proxy` and `kubelet` at
summary: A staged Kubernetes upgrade of CircleCI's main production cluster left `kube-proxy` and `kubelet` at incompatible versions. The change between versions altered the format of `kube-proxy`'s `iptables` rulesets, so as pods churned and `Endpoints` objects changed, `kube-proxy`'s `Proxier.syncProxyRules()` (an `iptables-save` / `iptables-restore` read-modify-write) repeatedly hit "Sync failed" errors, leaving the per-node iptables in a corrupted state and silently breaking service-to-service routing across the cluster. Recovery required a full node-by-node cluster restart and triggered two follow-on incidents.
fix: Restart the Kubernetes cluster node by node.

title: Cloudflare — A parser bug caused Cloudflare edge servers to return memory that contained private information such as
summary: A parser bug caused Cloudflare edge servers to return memory that contained private information such as HTTP cookies, authentication tokens, HTTP POST bodies, and other sensitive data.
fix: Disabled the affected HTML-rewriting features globally, deployed a patch to stop the parser memory leak, and worked with search engines to purge cached leaked data.
